title: So dar: the door, again
hookLine: so dar: what is that door where You sit and care for all, sung at dusk (Asa, ang 8–9)

lines: KEYS IN HAND AT YOUR OWN DOOR.
THE SAME DOOR, A DIFFERENT LIGHT.
cards: You come home in the evening and stop at your own front door, keys in hand. You've walked through it a thousand times.
But tonight you notice it: the scuff at the bottom, the light from inside showing round the edges, the sound of someone cooking. The same door you left by this morning looks different coming home.
Rehras opens with a door, and it's one the Japji already showed us at the start of the day.

teach.h: SO DAR KEHA: WHAT IS THAT DOOR?
teach.b: The first shabad of Rehras, by Guru Nanak in Raag Asa, opens with a question. So dar keha, so ghar keha: what is that door, what is that house, where You sit and take care of all?

Almost the same hymn is pauri twenty-seven of the Japji, the morning prayer. The Guru Granth Sahib carries it more than once, and Sikhs who keep the daily banis sing it at both ends of the day. At dawn, inside the Japji.

At dusk, as the first thing in Rehras. Then the shabad answers its own question, not with an address but with a crowd. Countless instruments play at that door, it says in paraphrase, and countless musicians.

teach.h: WIND, FIRE, SAINTS, WORLDS: ALL SINGING.
teach.b: Wind, water and fire sing. The gods of the old stories sing, and the record keepers of the dead, and the scholars, the warriors, the saints. Whole worlds and galaxies sing.
Those who please You sing, Guru Nanak says, steeped in love, and there are more than anyone could think of.

teach.h: THE KING OF KINGS; NANAK IN HIS WILL.
teach.b: And it closes on who sits at that door: the True One, who is and always will be, who made everything, who needs no one's orders, the King above kings. Nanak remains within His will.
So Rehras doesn't begin by asking for anything.
It begins by standing at the door at dusk and hearing that everything is already singing there. The door, again, at the other end of the day.

how: So Dar is the first shabad of Rehras Sahib, recited in the evening; a near-identical version is pauri 27 of the Japji in the morning, so many Sikhs sing this hymn at both ends of the day.

o: a doorway blessing hung over a Sikh home
the gurdwara's main gate, open on all sides
that door: where the One sits, and all sing

p: almost the same hymn, at dawn

s: the opening hymn of Rehras appears nowhere else in the Guru Granth Sahib
almost the same hymn is pauri 27 of the Japji, and it appears more than once.
the shabad answers its question with a list of who sings at the door
instruments, musicians, wind, water, fire, saints and whole worlds.
Rehras begins by asking for protection
it begins with praise: standing at the door and hearing everything already singing.

games.q: Guru Nanak asks: what is that door, that house, where You sit and care for all? how does the shabad answer?
o: it names a city and a temple.
it describes everything singing at that door.
it says the question can't be asked.
games.why: instead of an address, it gives a crowd: winds, fire, gods, saints and worlds, all singing, and the True King at the door.

practice: Picture the door you'll come through tonight, or stand near a real one, a front door, a bedroom door, an open window, and look at it as if for the first time. Notice the light on each side: the dusk out there, the lamps in here.
Stand, in your mind, on the line between them, where the shabad asks its question; if you pray, say Waheguru once.

wordCard.voice: So dar. That door: Guru Nanak's question that opens Rehras, sung also in the Japji. This week: pauri forty, every ceremony, the Anand at dusk and its close, Rehras, and now the door.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: so dar, that door; the opening words of Rehras and of Japji pauri 27.

carryVoice: Your line: the door at dusk. It's the same door the Japji opens at dawn. Until tomorrow, then.
